tagline.text: The largest mosque in Metro Manila, topped with a golden dome in Quiapo's Muslim quarter

location.label: Location
location.text: Globo de Oro Street, Quiapo, Manila

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Year-round (the December–May dry season is easiest for walking around Quiapo)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: 1–2 hours (half a day including the surrounding streets)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱0–500 (free entry; per person including transport, snacks and a halal meal)

children.text: The Manila Golden Mosque (Masjid Al-Dahab) stands on Globo de Oro Street, in Quiapo's Muslim quarter, and is considered the largest mosque in Metro Manila. It was built in 1976 and takes its name from its gold-painted dome. Entry is free, and non-Muslim visitors are welcome to look around quietly as long as they dress modestly and respect prayer times.

The Manila Golden Mosque is known in Arabic as Masjid Al-Dahab, in Filipino as Masjid Gintong, and in English as the Manila Golden Mosque and Cultural Center. It sits in the part of Quiapo, Manila, where many Muslim residents live, and Wikipedia describes it as the largest mosque in Metro Manila. "Al-Dahab" means gold in Arabic, and the name is said to come from both the gold-painted dome and Globo de Oro Street (Spanish for "golden globe"), where the mosque stands.

Its history goes back to 1976. According to Wikipedia, construction began on August 4, 1976, under the supervision of then First Lady Imelda Marcos. It was reportedly prepared for a visit by Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, but the visit was cancelled. Foreign donations, including from Libya and Saudi Arabia, paid for the construction. Its origins were political, but today it is a center of daily life for Manila's Muslim community, who pray here every day and gather for the Friday congregational prayer, Jumu'ah. Wikipedia says it can hold up to about 22,000 worshippers at Friday prayers.

The building's hallmark is its gold dome, about 12 meters across and 10 meters high. The geometric patterns are said to draw on the traditional art of the Maranao, Maguindanao and Tausug peoples of the southern Philippines, and the curved lines are based on the serpent motifs of Maranao art. The minaret that once stood here was torn down because of structural problems during the term of Mayor Lito Atienza, and the fundraising target for rebuilding it was reported to be ₱12 million. I could not find a source confirming whether it has been rebuilt, so it is best to see for yourself on site. Stained glass panels by the artist Antonio Dumlao were once displayed here as well, but they are now said to be at Far Eastern University.

For travelers, this is less a flashy attraction than a place to get close to Islamic culture in Manila. Quiapo Church, famous for the Black Nazarene devotion, is in the same district, so Catholic and Muslim faith live a few minutes' walk apart, which is one telling snapshot of Manila. Along Globo de Oro Street around the mosque you will find halal restaurants and shops selling traditional Mindanao Muslim goods, so a visit combines easily with lunch and some market browsing. Because it is a place of worship, be careful about photos, noise, clothing and prayer times, and since opening-hour information differs from source to source, it is safest to check locally in advance.

blocks.title: The golden dome and the Quiapo skyline

children.text: The gold dome, about 12 meters across, is the mosque's symbol and the source of its name. It stands out from far away among Quiapo's dense low-rise buildings. Many visitors say the gold looks warmest toward sunset.

blocks.title: The largest mosque in Metro Manila

children.text: Wikipedia names it the largest mosque in Metro Manila, and it is said to hold up to about 22,000 people at Friday congregational prayer. On ordinary days it is relatively quiet, and you can take in the prayer space with its line of columns at an easy pace.

Geometric patterns and curves drawn from Maranao, Maguindanao and Tausug traditional art are said to decorate the building. What sets it apart from other large mosques is that the art of the Philippines' Muslim peoples sits on top of a Middle Eastern-style dome.

Around noon on Friday, worshippers pour in and the street in front of the mosque fills with people. Going then lets you see the community's atmosphere, but it is hard for non-Muslims to enter the prayer space and you may be in the way. If you are only sightseeing, avoid prayer times and look from outside, quietly.

blocks.title: Halal eateries on Globo de Oro

children.text: Around the mosque are restaurants serving halal roast chicken and Maranao-style Mindanao dishes. One travel blog mentions places such as Moud's Chicken Halal and Junairah Halal Center and lists dishes such as pastil (chicken and rice wrapped in banana leaf), palapa and balbacua. Whether they are open and what they charge changes often.
Nearby shops sell traditional Mindanao Muslim cloth, caps and prayer items. Some travelers say prices are cheap, but they vary widely by item, so bargain politely.

Quiapo Church and Plaza Miranda are within walking distance. One blog describes the route from Carriedo Station past Quiapo Church, along Quezon Boulevard and through Quinta Market, then turning onto Globo de Oro. Seeing the church and the mosque in the same day lets you compare the two faces of Quiapo.

items.title: Half-day Quiapo route
items.subtitle: From the church to the mosque and a halal lunch

children.text: Get off at LRT-1 Carriedo Station and walk toward Quiapo. The streets are crowded, so carry your belongings in front of you.
Look around Plaza Miranda and the area around Quiapo Church. Church visits tend to run long, so set a time for the mosque and keep to it.
Pass Quezon Boulevard and Quinta Market and turn onto Globo de Oro Street. Once you see the street name, the gold dome will soon come into view.
Sort out your shoes and clothing in front of the mosque. The guard at the gate often gives directions, so follow them, and if it is prayer time, do not go in; wait or look around from outside.
Have lunch at a nearby halal restaurant. Ordering well-known dishes such as roast chicken or pastil is a safe choice. At noon on Fridays the area is jammed with worshippers, so adjust your timing.
Browse the Muslim goods shops and head back. Quiapo gets more crowded toward late afternoon, so it is better to call a taxi or Grab from a main road.
Prayer times around noon on Friday and the month of Ramadan may change visiting hours, so check the latest notices.

items.title: Full-day Quiapo religion and culture route
items.subtitle: Church, mosque and Intramuros

children.text: Start the morning at Quiapo Church. During Catholic services, look around quietly.
Move to Globo de Oro and view the mosque from outside first. Whether you can go inside depends on the on-site instructions.
Have lunch and rest at a halal restaurant.
Take a taxi or Grab to Intramuros and see San Agustin Church and Fort Santiago.
Head toward Manila Bay at sunset, or return to your hotel.

From anywhere in Manila, the easiest way is LRT-1. Get off at Carriedo Station and walk past Quiapo Church and Quezon Boulevard to Globo de Oro Street. Wikipedia places the mosque within walking distance southeast of Carriedo Station, and one guide site puts the walk at about 10 minutes.

Jeepneys, buses and UV Express vans run along Quezon Boulevard, Rizal Avenue and Carlos Palanca Sr. Street (Echague). Routes and fares change often, so check with the driver or signboards before boarding.
The streets in Quiapo are narrow and crowded, so getting anywhere by vehicle is very slow.
From Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA), a taxi or Grab is the most convenient. Travel time varies greatly with traffic, so check locally.
If you bring a car, park near Quinta Market. A 2014 blog said parking attendants charged about
, so it may have changed since.
A common way is to take a jeepney to Quiapo, get off on Quezon Boulevard and walk. Tricycles, padyak and kuligligs also run around the area.
Searching Google Maps for Masjid Al-Dahab or Manila Golden Mosque brings up the same spot.
You can visit the mosque year-round. However, Quiapo's streets are narrow and lined with stalls, so walking is uncomfortable on rainy days and you have to pass through crowded streets.

Worshippers flock here during the Islamic month of Ramadan, at Friday Jumu'ah prayers and during Eid festivals. These are good times to see the culture but can be inconvenient for sightseeing visits, so check the dates and times locally.

Quiapo is an old market district, so there are not many hotels that foreign travelers choose to stay in. Most people base themselves in Intramuros, Malate or Makati and visit for a day by taxi, Grab or LRT-1. At night Quiapo is chaotic and has dark alleys, so it is safer to leave before sunset.

Halal restaurants around the mosque suit it best for meals. Moud's Halal Roasted Chicken and Junairah Halal Center on Globo de Oro Street have been mentioned on blogs, along with Maranao-style dishes such as pastil, palapa and balbacua. Halal restaurants do not serve pork or alcohol, so choose with your group in mind. Places can change, so check recent reviews on Google Maps to see whether they are still open.
Wear clothing that covers your shoulders and knees. One guide site advises women to wear a headscarf and says one can sometimes be borrowed at the entrance. Bringing a small scarf is handy.
Take off your shoes before entering the prayer space. Shoes that are easy to remove are best.
Visiting hours differ by source: one lists 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. daily, another gives early morning and evening slots. Check the on-site notices before you go.
Reviews mention that prayer times are posted on the wall. Do not go in during prayers; wait.
Ask permission before taking photos. Avoid photographing people who are praying.
Keep quiet in the prayer space and do not eat there.
Entry is free, and if guards at the gate hand you an envelope, you can donate any amount you like. It is not required, so there is no need to feel pressured.
Worshippers pack the mosque at noon on Fridays, so if you are only sightseeing, a weekday morning is better.
This is a place of worship, so respect prayer times and dress rules, and Quiapo is an area where you should watch out for pickpockets and crowds.
Quiapo is crowded and pickpocketing does occur. Carry your bag in front and do not walk around with your phone out.
Do not walk alone at night. Call a taxi or Grab from a main road before dark.
Roads around the mosque get jammed at noon on Fridays and on Islamic holidays. Allow plenty of travel time.
Visiting hours and whether the interior is open differ by source. If it is closed, look from outside and do not force your way in.

The minaret was torn down, and whether it is rebuilt and the state of any repair work may change. In November 2025 Manila's mayor and the budget secretary announced a major rehabilitation of the mosque complex and a Halal Town plan, reportedly with UAE funding, but no start date or closure was confirmed, so check the latest news before you go.

Manila's Chinatown, reachable by taxi or Grab, lets you add Chinese-Filipino food and market browsing to the same day.
This walled city of the Spanish colonial era is a short taxi or Grab ride away. It makes a good follow-up, turning from Islamic culture to colonial history.
